lessons.title: How ISO standards work and the four you will meet
lessons.summary: You will be able to explain what an ISO standard asks for, tell the four common ones apart, and describe how a company gets and keeps a certificate.
lessons.why: Clients in medical devices and pharma will say 'we are ISO 13485 certified' or 'this has to meet ISO 14971' in the first meeting. Suppliers will ask whether your team holds ISO/IEC 27001. If you do not know what each standard covers and how it is checked, you will either over-promise or miss work that an auditor will later ask for. This lesson gives you the map.

p: A standard is an agreed document that describes a good way to do something. ISO (the International Organization for Standardization) publishes thousands of them, written by committees of experts from national standards bodies. The IEC (International Electrotechnical Commission) does the same for electrical and electronic topics, and some standards are written jointly, which is why you see names like ISO/IEC 27001.

A standard on its own is voluntary. It becomes binding when a law points to it, when a regulator recognises it, or when a customer writes it into a contract. In medical devices, regulators rely heavily on standards, so in practice they are close to mandatory.

Standards use a few words with exact meanings. 'Shall' is a requirement: if the standard says the organisation shall do something, an auditor will check that you do it. 'Should' is a recommendation: you may choose another way if you can justify it. 'May' gives permission, and 'can' describes a possibility.

Most requirements describe what must be achieved, not how. ISO 13485 says documents shall be reviewed and approved before issue; it does not say which software to use. That freedom is useful, but it means each company writes its own procedures, and you must read the client's procedures, not only the standard.

sections.h: The four standards you will meet
p: Three of these are management system standards: they describe how an organisation runs a set of processes, and a company can be certified against them. ISO 14971 is different: it describes a process for one product's risk, and is checked through audits and regulatory reviews of the product rather than certified on its own.
list: ISO 9001: quality management for any industry. It focuses on meeting customer requirements, risk-based thinking and continual improvement.

ISO 13485: quality management for medical devices. It is built on the same ideas but puts more weight on meeting regulatory requirements, documented procedures and keeping products safe and effective. The FDA QMSR incorporates ISO 13485:2016 by reference.
ISO 14971: risk management for medical devices. It sets out how to find hazards, estimate and evaluate risk, control it, judge what risk remains, and keep watching once the product is on the market.
ISO/IEC 27001: information security management. It asks the organisation to assess risks to its information, choose controls to treat them, and run the system so it keeps working.

p: ISO now writes its management system standards on a common skeleton, so ISO 9001 and ISO/IEC 27001 share the same main clause headings: context of the organisation, leadership, planning, support, operation, performance evaluation and improvement. That makes it easier to run several standards as one integrated system.

ISO 13485:2016 was written on the older ISO 9001 layout and does not follow this common skeleton, so clause numbers do not line up one to one with ISO 9001. When a client maps requirements between standards, expect a cross-reference table rather than an exact match.

ISO writes standards but does not certify anyone. Certification is done by independent certification bodies. A certification body is itself checked by a national accreditation body, and accreditation bodies that sign the International Accreditation Forum (IAF) multilateral recognition arrangement accept each other's work. A certificate from an accredited body therefore carries more weight than one from an unaccredited one.

The usual cycle is a stage 1 audit that checks the system is documented and ready, then a stage 2 audit that checks it is working in practice. If findings are closed, a certificate is issued, typically for three years, with surveillance audits in between and a recertification audit at the end.

sections.h: What working 'to ISO' means for an engineer
p: When a client says the work must be done 'to ISO', ask which standard, which edition and which of their procedures implement it. The standard rarely tells you what to do on Tuesday; the client's procedures do. Your job is to follow those procedures and leave records that show you did.

In practice that means a few habits. Use only approved, current versions of documents. Record who did what and when, for example who reviewed a test and who approved a change. Raise problems through the client's nonconformity or change process instead of fixing them quietly. Keep your own work in the controlled system the client names, not on a personal drive.

Finally, remember that a standard is one layer among several. A device maker also has to meet the law in each market it sells in, follow regulator guidance or justify not doing so, and keep the promises in its contracts. The next lessons show how to sort these layers and trace each requirement to evidence.

example.title: Worked example: which standards apply to one project (example scenario)
p: A device maker hires an engineering team to build a mobile app that reads values from a connected glucose meter and shows trends to the patient. The device maker is ISO 13485 certified. Before writing code, the team lead works out which standards touch the work.
The result is a short list the team can plan around, instead of a vague promise to 'follow ISO'.
list: ISO 13485: the app is part of a medical device, so its design and development must follow the device maker's design control procedures, which are written to meet ISO 13485.
ISO 14971: the app could show a wrong trend that leads to a wrong dose decision, so it needs hazards and risk controls in the product risk file.
ISO/IEC 27001: the app handles health data, and the device maker's contract asks suppliers to hold or align with ISO/IEC 27001 for information security.
ISO 9001: the engineering team's own company is ISO 9001 certified, which the device maker accepts as evidence for supplier quality, alongside its own supplier audit.
Not on the list but worth asking: software lifecycle requirements, usually met through IEC 62304, a separate IEC standard.

Fine, if the company also holds a current ISO 9001 certificate
Only after a stage 2 certification audit of the product itself
It is applied per product, not certified alone

The procedures replace the standard entirely once written
The standard says what; the procedures say how
Auditors never look at the standard during an audit

Surveillance audits by the certifier
A full stage 1 audit is repeated every single month
The company audits its certification body instead
questions.why: Certification bodies run surveillance audits during the cycle, then a recertification audit at the end.

lessons.title: ISO 9001 in practice
lessons.summary: You will be able to tell a regulation, a standard, a guidance document and a customer procedure apart, and trace an ISO 9001 requirement to the procedure and record that show it is met.
lessons.why: On a client project you will be handed a pile of documents: a law, two or three standards, some regulator guidance and a stack of the client's own procedures. They do not carry the same weight. If you treat guidance as law you over-build; if you treat a client procedure as optional you fail their audit. ISO 9001 is the simplest quality standard to learn this skill on, and many suppliers to MedTech and Pharma companies are certified to it.

sections.h: Four kinds of document, four kinds of weight
p: Before you read any standard, sort every document you are given into one of four groups. The group tells you whether something is mandatory, for whom, and who decides if it was met.

When two documents seem to disagree, the law comes first, then the customer contract and procedures, then the standard as written into them, then guidance. In practice a good client procedure already meets all the layers above it, so the procedure is usually the document you work from day to day.
list: Regulation: law made by a government, for example 21 CFR Part 820 (the FDA Quality Management System Regulation) or the EU Medical Device Regulation (EU) 2017/745. Mandatory for anyone it applies to. Enforced by the regulator.
Standard: a voluntary consensus document such as ISO 9001 or ISO 13485. It becomes binding when a law refers to it, a regulator recognises it, a certificate depends on it, or a contract names it.

Guidance: the regulator's current thinking on how to meet the law, such as an FDA guidance document or an EU MDCG document. FDA guidance states that it does not create legally binding requirements, but inspectors expect you to follow it or to justify a different approach.
Customer procedure: the client's own SOPs, work instructions and quality agreements. Binding on you through the contract, and the client's auditors will check you against them.

p: ISO 9001 sets requirements for a quality management system (QMS) in any industry: the way an organisation plans, runs, checks and improves its work so customers get what they asked for. Most certificates in use today name ISO 9001:2015, and this lesson uses that edition. In it, the requirements sit in clauses 4 to 10: context of the organisation, leadership, planning, support, operation, performance evaluation and improvement. A revised edition, ISO 9001:2026, was scheduled for publication in 2026 with a transition period for certified companies, so always check which edition a certificate or contract names before mapping clauses.

Context means the company decides which internal and external issues matter, who its interested parties are (customers, regulators, suppliers, staff) and what they need, and then writes down the scope of the QMS. Scope is important to you: if a site or a product line is outside the scope, the certificate says nothing about it.

sections.h: Process approach and plan, do, check, act
p: ISO 9001 asks the organisation to manage its work as connected processes, each with inputs, outputs, owners, measures and risks. Order handling, design, purchasing, production and customer feedback are typical processes. The output of one is the input to the next, which is why a fault in purchasing shows up later as a production problem.

Each process, and the system as a whole, runs on the plan, do, check, act (PDCA) cycle. Plan sets objectives and the way of working. Do carries it out. Check measures results against the plan, through monitoring, internal audit and management review. Act fixes what went wrong and improves. Clauses 6, 8, 9 and 10 map roughly onto plan, do, check and act.

ISO 9001 asks the organisation to think about what could stop it meeting its aims, and what opportunities exist, and to plan actions in proportion. It does not require a formal risk method. A simple table of risks per process, with an owner and an action, is often enough for a small company. This is different from ISO 14971, where product risk management follows a defined process.

Quality objectives must be measurable, monitored and communicated. 'Improve quality' is not an objective. 'Ship 98 percent of orders complete and on time, measured monthly' is one (an example figure, not a benchmark).

sections.h: Documented information: how much is enough
p: ISO 9001:2015 uses the phrase documented information for both documents (which say how to do something) and records (which prove it was done). It requires some specific records, such as evidence of competence, results of management review and records of nonconformities. Beyond that, the organisation decides what it needs to run its processes well.

So the right amount is the least that keeps work consistent and lets you prove what happened. An auditor will not fault a missing procedure if people work consistently and records exist. They will fault a beautiful procedure that nobody follows.

sections.h: Reading a clause through to the record
p: This is the core skill of the whole course. Take one requirement and follow it all the way down to evidence. You need legitimate access to the text: standards are copyrighted and sold, so use your client's licensed copy or buy your own. Do not paste standard text into public tools or shared drives.
list: Read the clause and underline every 'shall'. Each one is a separate requirement.
Write each requirement as an outcome in your own words, for example 'suppliers are evaluated and re-evaluated against criteria'.
Find the client procedure that implements it. Note its number and version.
Find the record that proves it happens, for example a supplier evaluation form for a named supplier.
Mark any gap: a 'shall' with no procedure, or a procedure with no records.

example.title: Worked example: a supplier evaluation requirement (fictional company)
p: A contract manufacturer of plastic housings is certified to ISO 9001. A device maker wants to use it as a supplier, and you are asked to check whether its supplier controls are real. You work from ISO 9001 clause 8.4, control of externally provided processes, products and services, using the device maker's licensed copy.
You underline the 'shall' statements and rewrite them as outcomes. You find the manufacturer's purchasing procedure and ask for evidence for two named resin suppliers.
list: Outcome: criteria exist for evaluating, selecting and re-evaluating suppliers. Procedure: purchasing procedure, section on approved suppliers. Record: scored evaluation forms for both resin suppliers. Status: met.
Outcome: results of evaluations are kept. Record: one resin supplier was last re-evaluated four years ago, while the procedure says every two years. Status: gap, the procedure is not followed.

Customer layer: the device maker's own supplier quality agreement asks for notice before any resin change. No such clause is in the manufacturer's procedure. Status: gap against the customer procedure, not against ISO 9001.
Output: a one-page map listing requirement, source type, procedure, record and status, with the two gaps flagged for the quality lead.

pitfalls: Treating FDA or EU guidance as if it were law, and building far more than needed. Guidance shows one acceptable way; a different justified way is allowed.
Assuming an ISO 9001 certificate covers the site or product you care about. Always read the scope statement on the certificate.
Writing a procedure for every clause and then not following it. Auditors check what people do and what the records show.
Reading only the standard and ignoring the client's procedures and quality agreements, which are the documents you will actually be audited against.

Both documents that guide work and records that prove it
Any email or chat message sent by the quality team over the last year

lessons.title: ISO 13485 for medical device quality
lessons.summary: You will be able to explain what ISO 13485 requires beyond ISO 9001, how it sits under device law in the US and EU, and which parts touch the software and data work an FDE does.
lessons.why: Almost every medical device client runs its QMS on ISO 13485. If you build a tool that handles complaints, design records or production data, that tool becomes part of their QMS, and its requirements become yours. Knowing which part of your work is driven by the law, which by the standard and which by the client's own SOP lets you scope validation and records correctly instead of guessing.

p: ISO 13485:2016 sets requirements for a quality management system for organisations involved in medical devices: manufacturers, and also suppliers, distributors and service providers. It shares many ideas with ISO 9001, but its aim is different. ISO 9001 aims at customer satisfaction and continual improvement. ISO 13485 aims at consistently making safe and effective devices and meeting regulatory requirements, and it asks the organisation to keep the system effective rather than to show constant improvement.

That regulatory focus runs through the text. Many clauses say the organisation shall do something 'in accordance with applicable regulatory requirements'. You cannot read ISO 13485 alone: you must also know which laws apply in each market the device is sold in.

sections.h: How it sits under device law
p: In the US, the FDA Quality Management System Regulation (QMSR, 21 CFR Part 820) took effect in February 2026 and incorporates ISO 13485:2016 by reference. So in the US, the ISO 13485 requirements are now part of the regulation for device makers it covers, plus some extra FDA requirements written in Part 820 itself. The FDA does not require an ISO 13485 certificate, and a certificate does not replace an FDA inspection.

In the EU, the Medical Device Regulation (EU) 2017/745 requires a quality management system. The harmonised European version of ISO 13485 is the usual way to show this, because meeting a harmonised standard gives a presumption of conformity with the matching legal requirements. A notified body audits the QMS as part of conformity assessment.
The pattern is the same in both: the law is the requirement, the standard is the agreed way to meet it, guidance explains the regulator's view, and the client's SOPs say how this company does it.
The structure looks familiar, but ISO 13485 asks for more documented procedures and more records. The parts you will meet most often are these.
list: Medical device file: for each device type or family, a file holding or pointing to its description, intended use, labelling, specifications and procedures for making, storing, installing and servicing it.
Design and development: planned stages with inputs, outputs, review, verification, validation, transfer to production and control of design changes, all recorded.
Purchasing: suppliers are evaluated and controlled in proportion to the risk of what they provide, and purchased product is verified.

Production: work is done under controlled conditions; processes whose output cannot be fully checked afterwards must be validated; products are identified and traced, with more traceability for implantable devices.
Software validation: computer software used in the QMS, and in production and service, must be validated for its intended use before first use and after changes, in proportion to risk.
Feedback and complaints: feedback is gathered as an early warning, complaints are handled to a documented procedure, and events that meet reporting criteria are reported to regulators.

p: Software validation is the clause most likely to land on your desk. If your tool helps decide whether a complaint is reportable, stores design history, or controls a production step, it is QMS or production software. The client will want evidence that it was validated for its intended use, with effort scaled to the risk. The FDA guidance on computer software assurance describes a risk-based way to do this, and it is guidance, so the client may justify another approach.

Records matter as much as function. Under the QMSR, electronic records are also subject to 21 CFR Part 11 where it applies. Ask early which records your tool creates, who signs them and how long they are kept, and read the client's own procedure for computerised systems. That procedure is what their auditors will hold you to.

Complaint handling is a closed loop. A complaint is received, recorded, evaluated for whether it must be reported to a regulator, investigated where needed, and linked to corrective action when a cause is found. In the US, Medical Device Reporting is set by 21 CFR Part 803, a regulation, with its own deadlines. The standard asks for the procedure; the law sets what and when to report; the client's SOP sets who decides.
Never let a tool decide reportability on its own. Automation can gather facts, draft a summary and flag a possible reportable event, but a trained person makes and records the decision.

Keep the loop traceable. Each complaint record should link to its investigation, any report made, and any corrective action, so an auditor can follow one complaint from receipt to closure without asking anyone to explain it.

example.title: Worked example: scoping a complaint intake assistant (fictional client)
p: A device maker selling in the US and EU asks for an assistant that reads incoming complaint emails, fills the complaint form in the QMS system and drafts a summary for the complaint handler. Before building, you map what applies, using the client's licensed copy of ISO 13485 and their SOPs.
list: Law: 21 CFR Part 820 (QMSR) for complaint handling through the incorporated standard; 21 CFR Part 803 for what must be reported to the FDA; the EU MDR for vigilance in the EU. Owner: regulatory affairs.
Standard: ISO 13485 requirements for complaint handling, reporting to regulators and validation of QMS software.
Guidance: FDA computer software assurance guidance for how much validation effort fits the risk.
Client procedure: complaint handling SOP and computerised system validation SOP. These set the form fields, the decision owner and the validation deliverables.

lessons.title: ISO 14971 at a practical level
lessons.summary: You will be able to follow the ISO 14971 risk process from plan to post-market, use its terms correctly, and see where your engineering work feeds the risk file.
lessons.why: Any feature you add to a medical device, or to software that supports one, can create or reduce risk to patients. Device clients will ask you to 'update the risk file' or 'add a risk control'. If you mix up hazard and harm, or treat a warning label as equal to a design fix, your change will be sent back. This lesson gives you the working vocabulary. It is introductory: leading a device risk assessment needs product, clinical and usability specialists.

sections.h: What ISO 14971 is and where it applies
p: ISO 14971:2019 describes a process for managing the risks of a medical device across its whole life, including software that is a device. It is a product process, not a management system: it is applied to each device, and its output is a risk management file for that device. It is not certified on its own. Auditors and regulators check it through the QMS audit, design reviews and premarket submissions.

A companion technical report, ISO/TR 24971, gives guidance on applying the standard. It is guidance, so it explains ways to meet the standard rather than adding requirements. The FDA lists recognised consensus standards in a public database, and you can search it to see how the FDA currently recognises ISO 14971.

Pharma uses a different document for the same idea. ICH Q9(R1) Quality Risk Management is an international guideline, published by the FDA as guidance, covering risk to product quality and so to patients in drug development and manufacturing. If your client makes drugs rather than devices, expect Q9, not ISO 14971.

ISO 14971 defines its terms carefully and reviewers expect you to use them the same way. Harm is injury or damage to the health of people, or damage to property or the environment. A hazard is a potential source of harm, such as electrical energy or wrong data. A hazardous situation is a circumstance in which people, property or the environment are exposed to a hazard. Risk is the combination of the probability that harm occurs and the severity of that harm.

These link in a chain: a hazard, through a sequence of events, leads to a hazardous situation, which may lead to harm. Writing the sequence of events is where engineers add the most value, because you know how the software or hardware can actually fail or be misused.

list: Plan: the risk management plan sets scope, responsibilities, the criteria for risk acceptability and the verification activities. Criteria come from the manufacturer's policy, not from the engineer on the day.
Analysis: state the intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse, list characteristics related to safety, identify hazards and hazardous situations, and estimate risk.
Evaluation: compare each estimated risk with the acceptability criteria in the plan.
Control: choose and implement controls, then verify that each was implemented and that it works.

Residual risk: evaluate the risk left after control, then the overall residual risk of the device; where it is not acceptable under the criteria, a benefit-risk analysis decides whether benefits outweigh it.
Review: before release, confirm the plan was carried out and the overall residual risk is acceptable.
Production and post-production: collect and review information from use, such as complaints and service data, and update the file when it shows new hazards or changed risk.
p: The process is a loop, not a one-off document. Every design change and every relevant complaint is a reason to open the file again.

sections.h: Order of preference for risk control
p: ISO 14971 sets an order for choosing controls. First, inherently safe design and manufacture: remove the hazard or make the failure impossible. Second, protective measures in the device itself or in manufacturing, such as an alarm, an interlock or an automatic check. Third, information for safety, such as warnings in labelling and, where appropriate, training.

The order matters because a warning depends on someone reading it at the right moment. If you propose a warning when a design change was practicable, a reviewer will ask why. Each control must also be checked for new risks it introduces: an extra alarm can cause alarm fatigue.

Engineers help identify failure modes, write the sequence of events, implement controls and produce verification evidence. Tools such as FMEA (failure mode and effects analysis) are often used inside the 14971 process, but an FMEA alone is not a risk management file because it starts from failures and can miss hazards that occur when everything works as designed, such as a correct but confusing display.

Your records should link both ways: from each risk control to the requirement and test that verify it, and from each requirement back to the risk it controls. That traceability is what lets the client show that the residual risk was judged on evidence.

Use errors deserve special care. Many hazardous situations start with a person misreading a screen or pressing the wrong button, not with a broken part. Usability engineering, described in IEC 62366-1 and in the FDA human factors guidance, feeds these use-related hazards into the risk file. If your feature changes what a user sees or does, ask the client whether it needs a usability review as well as a test.

example.title: Worked example: a dosage history screen (fictional device)
p: A home insulin pump has a companion app. You are asked to add a screen that shows the last 24 hours of doses. The client's risk file uses an example severity scale of 1 to 5 and an example probability scale of 1 to 5, defined in their plan. You draft entries for review by the risk owner.
list: Hazard: incorrect information shown to the user.
Sequence of events: the app shows cached data after the pump failed to sync; the user believes a dose was not given and gives a second dose.
Hazardous situation: user acts on stale dose history.
Harm: low blood sugar from a double dose. Severity and probability are scored by the clinical and risk owners under the plan, not by you.
Control 1, design: the screen will not show history older than the last successful sync without a clear 'not synced since' state. Verified by a test with the pump disconnected.
Control 2, information: a note in the instructions for use. Listed second because it relies on the user reading it.
Trace: each control links to a software requirement and a test case id, and the residual risk is left for the risk owner to evaluate.

lessons.title: ISO/IEC 27001 for engineering teams
lessons.summary: You will be able to explain how an ISMS chooses its controls, read a statement of applicability, and show the evidence an engineering team produces for one.
lessons.why: Clients will ask whether your team works inside their ISO/IEC 27001 scope, and their security team will send you a questionnaire before you touch any data. In MedTech and Pharma, the same data may also fall under device cybersecurity rules or GMP data integrity rules, which come from regulations and guidance rather than from ISO/IEC 27001. Knowing which driver applies stops you from answering a regulatory question with a certificate.

p: ISO/IEC 27001 sets requirements for an information security management system (ISMS): the policies, roles, processes and controls an organisation uses to protect the confidentiality, integrity and availability of its information. The current edition is ISO/IEC 27001:2022. It follows the same main clause structure as ISO 9001, so clauses 4 to 10 cover context, leadership, planning, support, operation, performance evaluation and improvement.

The core idea is that controls are chosen from risk, not from a checklist. The organisation decides its scope, assesses risks to its information, picks controls to treat them, and keeps checking that the controls work. Like ISO 9001, it is a management system standard, so a company can be certified against it by an accredited certification body.

The organisation defines how it will assess risk, with criteria for acceptance, so that repeated assessments give comparable results. It then identifies risks to information in scope, names an owner for each, judges likelihood and consequence, and decides on treatment.

Treatment usually means one of four things: reduce the risk with controls, avoid it by not doing the activity, share it, for example with an insurer or a supplier contract, or accept it. Risk owners approve the treatment plan and accept the residual risk. As an engineer you will mostly implement the controls and provide evidence that they run.

sections.h: Annex A and the statement of applicability
p: Annex A of ISO/IEC 27001:2022 lists 93 reference controls grouped into four themes: organisational, people, physical and technological. ISO/IEC 27002 is a separate guidance standard that explains each control in more depth. The organisation compares the controls it chose from risk against Annex A to make sure nothing necessary was missed.

The result is the statement of applicability (SoA). For each Annex A control it says whether the control is included, why, whether it is implemented, and why any control is excluded. The SoA is the best single document to read when you join a client: it tells you which controls they claim to run and therefore what evidence an auditor will expect from your work.

list: Access control: least privilege, named accounts, approval before access, and periodic access reviews with a record of who reviewed what.
Logging and monitoring: security-relevant events are logged, logs are protected from change, and someone looks at them.
Secure development: a defined secure development life cycle, secure coding rules, security testing before release and control of changes.
Supplier security: cloud services, APIs and libraries are assessed and covered by agreements, and their use is monitored.
Configuration and secrets: hardened settings, no secrets in code, keys rotated and stored in an approved vault.
Incident handling: you know how to report a suspected incident in the client's process, and you do it quickly.
p: Each of these should leave a record you could show an auditor: a ticket, a review sign-off, a pipeline log or a test report.

sections.h: Three different drivers for security work
p: In regulated clients, three separate things are often all called 'security'. Keep them apart, because each comes from a different kind of document and has a different owner.

ISMS security protects the organisation's information and is driven by ISO/IEC 27001, a voluntary standard that becomes binding through certification or contracts. Medical device cybersecurity protects the device and its patients; in the US it is driven by law for cyber devices and explained in FDA premarket cybersecurity guidance. GMP data integrity protects the reliability of records used for drug quality decisions; it is driven by regulations such as 21 CFR Part 11 and the drug GMP rules, and explained in FDA data integrity guidance. One control, such as an audit trail, can serve all three, but the evidence and the reviewer differ.

sections.h: Your first week inside a client ISMS
p: Start by asking for three things: the ISMS scope statement, the statement of applicability rows that touch your work, and the security procedures your team must follow, such as access requests, change management and incident reporting. These are customer procedures, and they bind you through the contract even where the standard itself is silent.

Then agree, in writing, which records your team will produce and where they will live. Auditors sample evidence from the period being audited, so a record created months later to fill a gap is weak and can look like falsification. Finally, find out who owns security risk for your system. When you find a new risk, such as a library with a known vulnerability, you raise it to that owner instead of deciding alone whether it is acceptable.

example.title: Worked example: a data pipeline inside a client ISMS (fictional client)
p: A pharma client certified to ISO/IEC 27001 asks your team to build a pipeline that copies batch quality data into an analytics store. Their security lead sends you the relevant rows of their SoA and asks for an evidence plan before go-live.
list: SoA row, access control: included. Your evidence: named service accounts, access request tickets, and a quarterly access review record.
SoA row, logging: included. Your evidence: pipeline and database logs sent to the client's log platform, with retention set by their procedure.
SoA row, secure development: included. Your evidence: code review records, dependency scan results and a change ticket per release.
SoA row, supplier security: included. Your evidence: confirmation that the analytics service is on the client's approved supplier list.
Separate driver: batch quality data are GMP records, so the client's data integrity and computerised system procedures also apply. That needs the quality unit's review, not only the security lead's.
Output: a table with control, source type, owner, evidence and status, shared with both security and quality.

lessons.title: Audits and certification
lessons.summary: You will be able to tell audit types apart, read and write a finding that cites the correct requirement, and support an audit with clear evidence.
lessons.why: Sooner or later an auditor will sit next to you and ask to see how a change to your tool was approved. Clients also audit their suppliers, which may include your team. If you know what an auditor is looking for and how findings are graded, you can prepare the right records in advance and answer calmly. If you cannot tell a standard requirement from a client procedure, you will argue with findings that are valid or accept ones that are not.

p: An audit is a planned, independent check of whether work meets defined criteria, based on objective evidence. There are three kinds, named by who does it.
list: First party: an internal audit, done by the organisation on itself, often by trained staff from another department.
Second party: a customer audits a supplier, usually against the contract, the quality agreement and the standards they name.
Third party: an independent certification body audits against a standard such as ISO 13485 or ISO/IEC 27001 and issues or keeps a certificate.

p: A regulatory inspection is different. The FDA or another regulator inspects against the law, and its findings can lead to enforcement. At the end of an FDA inspection, an investigator may issue Form 483, which lists observations of conditions that may break the law. Responding to a 483 or a warning letter is specialist work for the client's quality and regulatory leads; this lesson does not prepare you to lead it.

The Medical Device Single Audit Program (MDSAP) sits in between. Recognised auditing organisations perform one audit of a device maker's QMS that several regulators, including the FDA, can use. It is still built on ISO 13485 plus each country's specific rules.

The auditor agrees a scope, criteria and a plan with the auditee, then opens with a short meeting. Most of the time is spent sampling: the auditor picks a few records, such as three change requests from the last six months, and follows each through the process. They are looking for objective evidence, meaning records, observations and statements that can be checked, not opinions. ISO 19011 gives guidance on auditing management systems and is a good source for how auditors are trained to think.

At the closing meeting, the auditor presents findings. Each finding must name the requirement, the evidence and what was wrong. The requirement can come from a regulation, a standard or the organisation's own procedure, and a good finding says which.

Sampling cuts both ways. A clean sample does not prove every record is right, and one bad sample does not prove the whole process is broken. That is why auditors describe findings by how many samples failed, and why the response should check whether the problem is wider than the sample.

Certification bodies usually grade a nonconformity as major or minor. A major nonconformity puts in doubt the system's ability to achieve its intended results, for example a required process missing entirely, and usually blocks or suspends certification until it is corrected. A minor one is a lapse that does not, such as one record missing a signature. Auditors may also note opportunities for improvement, which do not need action. Exact definitions and deadlines come from the certification body's own rules.

The response follows CAPA (corrective and preventive action): fix the immediate problem (correction), find the root cause, act on the cause so it does not recur (corrective action), and check later that the action worked. Retraining one person is rarely an adequate root cause fix on its own.

Certification starts with a stage 1 audit, which checks that the system is documented, scoped and ready. A stage 2 audit then checks that it works in practice. When findings are closed, the certificate is issued, typically for three years. Surveillance audits, usually yearly, sample parts of the system, and a recertification audit before expiry renews it. Certification bodies should themselves be accredited, which you can check through the International Accreditation Forum and its members.

Regulated clients often hold several certificates and face several regulators, so audits rarely stop. Ask the quality lead for the audit calendar early. Knowing that a surveillance audit is due next month tells you which records to tidy now, while there is still time to fix gaps honestly through the normal process.

list: Answer the question asked, with evidence. Show the record rather than describe it.
If you do not know, say so and offer to find out. Never guess or invent an answer.
Keep records in the controlled system so you can find them in under a minute.
Do not create or back-date records during the audit to fill a gap. Report the gap instead.
Disagree politely and with evidence if a finding cites the wrong requirement.
p: Auditors judge the system, not you personally. A calm, honest auditee who shows clear records makes the audit shorter for everyone.

example.title: Worked example: writing a finding with the right source (fictional client)
p: You are on an internal audit team at a device maker. The client's change control SOP says every software change to a QMS tool needs approval from quality before release. You sample five changes to the complaint tool from the last quarter. Four have quality approval. One was released on a Friday with only the developer's approval, and the change ticket says 'urgent fix'.
list: Requirement: client change control SOP, approval before release (customer procedure), which implements the ISO 13485 requirement to control changes to QMS software (standard).
Objective evidence: change ticket for release 2.3.1, approval history shows developer only, deployment log shows release before any quality sign-off.
Statement: one of five sampled changes was released without the quality approval required by the SOP.
Grade: minor, because the process exists and works in four of five samples. A missing process would be major.

Expected response: correction (retrospective review of release 2.3.1), root cause (no documented emergency change path), corrective action (add one and block deployment without approval), effectiveness check (sample changes next quarter).

practice.title: Run a mini audit on your own records
practice.goal: Practise sampling, objective evidence and writing a finding.
steps: Pick a rule you or your team claims to follow, such as 'every pull request is reviewed before merge' in a GitHub repository you can see.
Write the rule down as the audit criterion and note its source type: law, standard, customer procedure or team habit.
Sample five recent merges and record, for each, who approved it and when, compared with the merge time.
Write any finding in three parts: requirement, objective evidence, statement. Grade it major or minor and explain why.
Draft a CAPA: correction, root cause, corrective action and how you would check it worked.
Ask Claude to critique whether your finding is based on evidence rather than opinion.
practice.done_when: You have a five-row sample table and either a written, graded finding with a CAPA draft, or a written conclusion that the rule was met with the evidence listed.

pitfalls: Creating or back-dating records during an audit to cover a gap. That turns a small finding into a data integrity problem.
Writing findings as opinions, such as 'change control is weak'. A finding needs a requirement, objective evidence and a clear statement.
Citing the standard when the real requirement is the client's own procedure, or the reverse, which makes the finding easy to dispute.
Closing every finding with 'retrain the person'. Look for the process cause, such as a missing emergency path, and check effectiveness later.
Treating a certificate as proof of regulatory compliance. Regulators inspect against the law and do not rely on certificates.

lessons.title: Running several standards as one system
lessons.summary: You will be able to justify whether a standard applies to a piece of work, map its requirements to procedures and evidence, and keep that map current when things change.
lessons.why: A typical MedTech or Pharma client lives under several laws, several standards, regulator guidance and hundreds of its own procedures at once. Nobody runs these as separate systems; they run one system that answers to all of them. As an FDE you will be asked which requirements apply to your tool and what evidence you will produce. A clear applicability and evidence map is the answer, and it is the main skill this course builds.

p: ISO writes its management system standards on a common high-level structure, set out in Annex SL of the ISO/IEC Directives and now called the harmonized structure. ISO 9001, ISO 14001 (environment), ISO 45001 (occupational health and safety) and ISO/IEC 27001 all use it. They share the same main clauses, many identical core definitions and much identical core text, such as the requirements for context, leadership, internal audit and management review.

So a company can run one document control process, one internal audit programme and one management review that serve every standard. ISO 13485:2016 is the exception you will meet most: it follows the older ISO 9001 layout, so its clauses need a cross-reference table rather than a direct match. Pharma companies add another layer: their pharmaceutical quality system is driven by GMP law and described by the ICH Q10 guideline, which is not an ISO standard at all.
Before mapping anything, justify why the standard applies to this work. Write the reason down, because a reviewer will ask. A standard applies when one or more of these is true.
list: A law makes it part of the requirement, for example the QMSR incorporating ISO 13485 by reference.
A regulator recognises it as a way to show conformity, for example an FDA recognised consensus standard or an EU harmonised standard, and the client chose to use it.
The client is certified to it and your work falls inside the certificate scope.
A contract or quality agreement names it.
The client's own procedure adopts it as their method, for example ISO 14971 for product risk.

p: Always record the edition, such as ISO/IEC 27001:2022, not just the number. Regulators and certificates point to specific editions, and transition periods apply when a new one is published. Check the status in an official source: the FDA recognised standards database for US device work, the European Commission lists for EU harmonised standards, or the client's own register of standards. Do not rely on memory or on a summary written by someone else.
You also need legitimate access to the text. Standards are copyrighted. Use the client's licensed copy through their approved system, and keep quotations in your map short.

Guidance documents have status too. FDA guidance can be draft or final, and a newer version can replace an older one. EU MDCG documents are endorsed guidance, not law. Record the version and date you used in the map, so a reviewer can see which text your decisions were based on.

sections.h: Building the applicability and evidence map
p: The map is a table with one row per requirement. It joins every layer you have learned in this course, so a reviewer can follow any requirement from source to proof.
list: Requirement: the clause or section reference and a short outcome in your own words.
Source type: regulation, standard, guidance or customer procedure.
Applies: yes, no or partly, with the reason.
Implemented by: the client procedure or system feature, with version.
Evidence: the record that proves it, and where it is kept.
Owner and status: who is accountable, and met, gap or not yet due.

sections.h: Keeping the map current through change
p: A map is only useful if it changes when the world does. Three kinds of change should trigger a review: a new edition of a standard or a new regulation or guidance; a change to the client's procedures; and a change to your own tool or process. For each, filter the map for affected rows, update the procedure and evidence columns, and record the review through the client's change control. This is also how combined audits stay efficient: one auditor can sample one set of records and test several standards at once, because the map shows which requirements each record supports.

Change also flows the other way. When your tool changes, the map tells you which records may need to be redone, for example a validation test that covered the old behaviour. That is the change impact view a quality reviewer will ask for before approving a release.

sections.h: Where AI helps and where it does not
p: An approved AI tool can speed up the slow parts: suggesting likely matches between two standards, finding which client procedures mention a topic, or drafting the outcome wording for a clause. Use it only on text you are licensed to process, inside a tool the client has approved for that data.

It cannot decide applicability, and it can invent clause numbers or merge similar requirements that are actually different. Treat every suggested row as a draft. A person checks each reference against the source text, confirms the evidence exists, and signs off the map.

example.title: Worked example: a CAPA drafting assistant (fictional client)
p: A device maker certified to ISO 13485 and ISO/IEC 27001 asks your team to build an assistant that drafts CAPA investigation summaries from linked complaint and nonconformity records. A quality engineer reviews and approves each draft. You build the map before writing code.
list: 21 CFR Part 820 (regulation): applies, because the client sells in the US and CAPA is part of the QMS. Implemented by: client CAPA SOP. Evidence: approved CAPA records.

ISO 13485:2016 (standard): applies by reference in the QMSR and by certificate scope. Requirement: validate QMS software for its intended use. Implemented by: client computerised system validation SOP. Evidence: validation plan and report for the assistant.
FDA computer software assurance guidance (guidance): adopted by the client's validation SOP as the method for sizing effort. Evidence: risk assessment in the validation plan.

ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (standard): applies by certificate scope, since the assistant processes complaint data. Implemented by: access request and logging procedures. Evidence: access tickets and log configuration.
Client CAPA SOP (customer procedure): requires a named human approver for every investigation. Implemented by: approval step in the QMS. Evidence: approval history per CAPA.
ISO 9001: does not apply. Not referenced by law, not in scope, not in the contract. Recorded as not applicable with the reason.

practice.title: Build an applicability and evidence map for one source
practice.goal: Produce the core output of this course on freely available text.
steps: Open 21 CFR Part 11 on eCFR and read the controls for closed systems in subpart B.
Pick a system you know that holds records, such as a shared document tool or a ticketing system, and imagine it holds GMP records at a pharma client.
Write a one-paragraph applicability statement: why Part 11 would apply, citing the source type.
In a spreadsheet with the six map columns from this lesson, add five rows for five requirements in subpart B.
For each row, name the system feature or procedure that would meet it and the record that would prove it, and mark it met, gap or unknown.
Ask Claude to review your map, then check every reference it questions against the eCFR text yourself before changing anything.
practice.done_when: You have a written applicability statement and five complete map rows, each with a source reference you checked on eCFR and a named evidence record.

pitfalls: Mapping a standard before writing down why it applies. Without the reason, nobody can tell whether the work is needed.
Recording a standard number without its edition. Regulators and certificates point to specific editions.
Copying an AI-suggested cross-reference into the map without checking each clause against the licensed text.
Running separate document sets for each standard, which creates conflicting procedures and doubles audit effort.
Treating the map as finished at go-live. New editions, procedure changes and tool changes should all trigger a review.
